growth_story.headline: Lebanon's income per person is 39.8 percent below its 2010 peak, after war next door, a banking collapse and renewed conflict undid three decades of gains.
growth_story.arc: After the civil war, Lebanon's income per person grew 14.0 percent a year from 1990 to 1997, partly a rebound from a deep fall in 1989, as rebuilding drew in large capital inflows. Growth slowed to 2.7 percent a year from 1998 to 2012, with a burst of 6.9 to 8.8 percent a year from 2007 to 2010 that carried income per person to its 2010 peak; the sources opened here do not explain that burst. From 2013 to 2024 income per person shrank 3.9 percent a year. The war in Syria hit tourism, confidence and public services first, then a banking and currency crisis that broke in 2019 brought a fall of 20.1 percent in 2020. As conflict returned, income per person fell a further 7.6 percent in 2024, leaving it about where it first was in 1994.

threads.title: Rebuilding after the civil war
threads.text: The 1990s boom was a postwar rebuilding of damaged roads, power and ports. It was paid for by large capital inflows, drawn by high interest rates and a stable exchange rate, and by fast-rising public debt.

threads.title: Spillover from Syria's war
threads.text: From 2012 the war in Syria hurt tourism and confidence, and a large influx of refugees put public services under strain. The World Bank described a heavy toll on the economy, its social fabric and public services, as income per person began to fall in 2013.

threads.title: A financial system that collapsed
threads.text: The World Bank describes years of borrowing that kept deposits flowing in and gave an illusion of stability, until the system broke in 2019. Banks stopped lending and savers lost access to their deposits, and investment fell from 21.8 percent of GDP in 2018 to 1.4 in 2024. Years on, the banking sector is still deeply weakened.

since_last_year.text: The World Bank reported a rebound in 2025, led by private spending, and inflation fell from 221.3 percent in 2023 to 14.6 in 2025. The March 2026 escalation of conflict reversed the rebound: the World Bank now expects the economy to shrink in 2026, and the IMF said in September 2026 that activity will contract significantly. By September 2026, amendments to the law for resolving failed banks had been approved, which the IMF called a significant step in restructuring the banks.

growth_story.tension: The data's 14.0 percent a year for 1990 to 1997 owes much to bouncing back from 1989, when income per person fell 43.6 percent, so it overstates the postwar pace the IMF describes for GDP. In 2013 the World Bank described an economy that was slowing, not shrinking, yet income per person fell 5.4 percent in 2013 and 7.3 in 2014; the refugee influx the sources describe likely enlarged the population sharing the same output. And the World Bank reports growth in 2025 that the data, which end in 2024, do not yet show.
